clue.text: Legendary hack, Ulster Jack joins trendy broadcaster

parts.note: NI, Northern Ireland, is often called Ulster
J is the card abbreviation for jack
in means fashionable
Sky is a British satellite broadcaster

explanation.surface: A famous journalist from Northern Ireland joining a fashionable TV channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hack' suggests a journalist in this magazine, but here it is a horse. Nijinsky won the English Triple Crown in 1970.
explanation.definitionFit: A hack is also a horse, and Nijinsky was a celebrated racehorse, hence a legendary one.

clue.text: Shock Sixties musical

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a shock is a thick mass of head ...
second meaning: the 1967 rock musical about hippies

explanation.walkthrough: 'Shock' looks like surprise, but it is a mop of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a thick shaggy head of tresses and the famous rock musical of 1960s counterculture.

clue.text: A load of bollocks, but Cyclops owns this entire mag

definitions.meaning: first meaning: nonsense, from the old idiom for something not to be believed
second meaning: the setter Cyclops claims the whole of Private Eye is his

explanation.walkthrough: The magazine is Private Eye, so Cyclops claiming it all would say the phrase literally. 'All my eye and Betty Martin' is an old British expression for nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means rubbish or humbug, and read literally it is a boast of owning the whole Eye.

clue.text: Kelvin on NASA's liberal state

parts.note: K is the symbol for the kelvin temperature unit

indicators.note: liberal suggests free and loose handling, so the letters of NASA's are rearranged

explanation.surface: A scientist named Kelvin working on NASA's progressive state.
explanation.definitionFit: Kansas is one of the fifty states of the USA, in the Midwest.

clue.text: Flatulence takes a different route, apparently, around autumn — a bonus for Gordon?

indicators.note: around tells us the first two pieces sit either side of the season word

parts.note: flatulence is wind in the gut

indicators.note: apparently signals that only the sound of the phrase counts, not its spelling

parts.note: a sailing boat that tacks changes course, so this phrase gives TACKS
in American usage autumn is the fall

explanation.surface: A comic picture of wind blowing off course, tacked onto a sly dig at the Chancellor's budget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apparently' says only the sound counts: a boat that tacks takes a different route, heard as TAX. 'Around' puts that and the flatulence either side of autumn. Brown, Chancellor from 1997, taxed utilities' excess profits.
explanation.definitionFit: Brown's levy on utility profits was a windfall to the Treasury, hence a bonus from Gordon's point of view.

clue.text: Arse-over-tip Heath, mounting beefy bloke, gets lush treatment

indicators.note: arse over tip means head over heels, upside down, so the name is turned backwards

parts.note: Ted Heath was a British Conservative Prime Minister
an ox is beefy; mounting says the turned name sits on top of it in this down clue

explanation.surface: Private Eye innuendo: Ted Heath tumbling onto a hunk on his way to rehab.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arse-over-tip' turns TED into DET. A lush is a heavy drinker; Ted Heath was a British Prime Minister.
explanation.definitionFit: A drying-out programme for an alcoholic, a lush, is detoxification, shortened.

clue.text: Our hackette provides Labour's star minister with flipping good western women

parts.note: Glenda Jackson, the film star who became a Labour minister in 1997

indicators.note: flipping means the following pieces are turned round

parts.note: gals is the folksy, Wild West word for women

explanation.surface: A hackette supplies a Labour celebrity minister with women of dubious virtue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' turns G + GALS round to SLAGG. Glenda Slagg is Private Eye's spoof female columnist, so 'Our' means the magazine's.
explanation.definitionFit: Glenda Slagg is the Eye's parody of a gushing tabloid woman columnist, a female hack.

clue.text: Knockers uniting and getting enduringly close to one another

definitions.text: getting enduringly close to one another

parts.note: knockers is slang for breasts, which come as a pair
bonding is joining or uniting

explanation.surface: A cleavage pressed together into lasting closeness.
explanation.definitionFit: Pair bonding is the formation of a lasting attachment between two partners, a zoological and social term.

clue.text: About to live with outed tories somewhere sheltered from reality!

parts.note: C is short for circa, about
L marks the live terminal on an electric plug

indicators.note: outed tories are exposed and turned out, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A jibe at Tory MPs forced out of the closet and hiding from the world.
explanation.walkthrough: L for live is the electric plug convention; 'outed' shuffles it with TORIES into LOISTER, and does double duty as Labour's 1997 rout of the Tories and the exposing of secrets.
explanation.definitionFit: A cloister is a monastery walkway, and by extension any life secluded from the world outside.

clue.text: Spare supermodel needs publicity agency

parts.note: Kate Moss, the famously thin (spare) supermodel
an ad, an advertisement, is publicity

explanation.surface: A skinny supermodel looking for a PR firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spare' here means lean, the word often used of Kate Moss's waif look.
explanation.definitionFit: Mossad is Israel's intelligence service, a secret agency.

clue.text: Gordonstoun is expressly concealing what 'Charlie' is gender-wise

indicators.note: concealing means the letters sit inside the run of words Gordonstoun is expressly

parts.note: the letters run across the end of Gordonstoun, all of is and the start of expressly

explanation.surface: A dig at Prince Charles, educated at Gordonstoun school, and his sexuality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concealing' says the answer lies inside the first three words. Gordonstoun is the Scottish boarding school Prince Charles attended, which makes 'Charlie' look like him.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlie was a popular Revlon fragrance, and something unisex suits either sex.

clue.text: Test interrupted by 'silly arse' (as all can see) Brown's lot

indicators.note: interrupted by means the next pieces break into the word for test

parts.note: to try is to test

indicators.note: silly means the letters of arse are jumbled

parts.note: U is the film certificate for a universal audience that anyone may see

explanation.surface: A silly ass barging in on Gordon Brown's team mid-exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silly' is the anagram signal on arse, giving REAS, and 'interrupted by' means the test word is split around it and the U. The U certificate marks a film suitable for everyone. Brown was Chancellor of the Exchequer in 1997.
explanation.definitionFit: As Chancellor, Brown ran the Treasury, the government department that was his lot or charge.

clue.text: Maxim awards X to film

parts.note: X is the Roman numeral ten
E.T. is Spielberg's 1982 film

explanation.surface: Maxim magazine handing out an X-rating to a film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maxim' looks like the men's magazine and X like a film rating, but X is ten given to the film E.T.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenet is a principle or belief, much like a maxim or guiding rule.

clue.text: Sailors against being taken out by the working man

indicators.note: being taken out tells us one letter is removed from the labourer's word

parts.note: a navvy is a labourer on roads or railways
v, versus, means against

explanation.surface: Sailors objecting to being thrown out by a labourer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being taken out' removes one V (against, versus) from NAVVY, a British word for a manual labourer.
explanation.definitionFit: A navy is a country's sea force, its body of sailors.

clue.text: 'Behave like a puff' acceptable in politically correct English?

indicators.note: in places the acceptable word inside the abbreviations

parts.note: something that is on is acceptable, as in that's not on

explanation.surface: Asking whether a homophobic slur is acceptable in politically correct speech.
explanation.walkthrough: ON sits inside PCE. Puff and ponce are dated British slang, here for showing off in a camp way.
explanation.definitionFit: To ponce about is British slang for parading in an affected, effeminate manner.

clue.text: Hacks before nazi paramilitary johnnies?

parts.note: pre is a prefix meaning before
the SS was the Nazi paramilitary force
johnnies is old British slang for chaps, men

explanation.surface: Journalists ahead of stormtroopers carrying condoms, johnny being slang for a condom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Johnnies' hints at condoms, but here it is the older sense of fellows.
explanation.definitionFit: Pressmen are newspaper reporters, and hack is a slang term for a journalist.

clue.text: Our distinguished columnist's bottom

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Paul ..., the campaigning journalist who wrote for Private Eye
second meaning: the ... of something is its lowest part

explanation.walkthrough: 'Our' is Private Eye speaking: Paul Foot was its long-standing investigative columnist.
explanation.definitionFit: Foot is both the surname of the Eye's investigative writer and the word for the base or lowest point of a page or hill.

clue.text: Party forfeit: one penetrates posh girl

parts.note: a fine is a penalty forfeited

indicators.note: penetrates means the letter for one goes inside the girl word

parts.note: gel is how an upper-class speaker says girl
A means one, as in a single

explanation.surface: A saucy party game where losing a forfeit involves a posh girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine Gael is a major political party in the Republic of Ireland.

clue.text: Minister takes PM (broadcast ditched) on topless publicly-funded spree with Tory leader

indicators.note: ditched means the broadcast word is dropped from the Prime Minister's name

parts.note: Tony Blair was Prime Minister from 1997
to air something is to broadcast it

indicators.note: topless means the first letter of the spree word is cut off

parts.note: a junket is a trip enjoyed at public expense

indicators.note: leader picks the first letter of Tory

parts.note: taken from Tory

explanation.surface: A minister enjoying a taxpayer-funded jolly with the Prime Minister and a Tory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ditched' drops AIR from BLAIR to leave BL, 'topless' cuts JUNKET to UNKET, and 'leader' takes T from Tory. David Blunkett was Education Secretary in 1997.
explanation.definitionFit: David Blunkett served as a cabinet minister in Blair's government, so he is an example of a minister.

clue.text: Heroin-injector's prick?

parts.note: what punctures the skin of a drug user is the sharp point of a syringe, though prick suggests a person

explanation.walkthrough: 'Prick' tempts as an insult for the addict, but it is the sharp tool that makes the puncture.
explanation.definitionFit: A hypodermic's sharp point pricks the skin, so it is the user's instrument for pricking.

clue.text: Country prison, commercial grade

parts.note: the can is slang for prison
a commercial is an advert, an ad
A is a top grade in exams

explanation.surface: A rural jail graded like a business.
explanation.definitionFit: Canada is a nation in North America, an example of a country.

clue.text: Following ex-PM is the role of this court serenader

definitions.text: Following ex-PM is the role of this
definitions.meaning: first meaning: placed after the ex-PM Heath, this word makes Heathcliff, the role its owner played
second meaning: ... Richard, who sang to the Wimbledon crowd on Centre Court during a rain delay in 1996

explanation.walkthrough: Cliff Richard starred in the musical Heathcliff in 1996-97, so his name follows HEATH (Ted Heath) to give his role.
explanation.definitionFit: The pop singer Cliff Richard is famous both for that stage role and for serenading the tennis crowd at Wimbledon.

clue.text: Fabulously big female casually rogers topless Bob

indicators.note: casually means the remaining letters are arranged loosely
topless means the first letter of rogers is removed

parts.note: taken as written
a bob was a shilling in old British money, abbreviated s

explanation.surface: A large woman casually bedding a shirtless man named Bob.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' leaves OGERS and 'casually' turns it into OGRES. 'Rogers' is British slang for has sex with, and 'Bob' looks like a name but is the old shilling.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogress is a female giant of fairy tales, so a big woman of fable.

clue.text: Being an active trendy type is deeply affecting without Ecstasy

indicators.note: without means the drug letter is removed

parts.note: swingeing means severe, hitting hard
E is street slang for the drug Ecstasy

explanation.surface: A clubber's lament that being hip is a heavy burden without drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' removes the E (Ecstasy) from swingeing, a British word chiefly used of severe cuts.
explanation.definitionFit: Swinging describes a lively, fashionable lifestyle, as in the Swinging Sixties.

clue.text: Tabloid with end of week supplement got even lower

indicators.note: supplement means the last piece is added on after the tabloid

parts.note: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper

indicators.note: end of picks the last letter of week

parts.note: taken from week

explanation.surface: A dig at a downmarket paper adding a weekend supplement and sinking lower still.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunk is a past form of sink, to descend, so it means went down further.

clue.text: One with the potential to form a bond with the source of his addiction?

definitions.text: One with the potential to form a bond with the source of his addiction?

parts.words: One with the potential to form a bond with the source of his addiction
parts.note: the addict's substance is adhesive, which is literally designed to form a bond

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a therapy session about an addict's emotional attachment; the bond is a literal one made by adhesive.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who inhales solvent vapour from adhesive for a high is addicted to a substance used for bonding.
